doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Organ work, singers and Russia tour
title: Touring the Soviet Union with the New York Jazz Repertory Company, 1975
summary: Hyman led the Louis Armstrong show through Moscow and Central Asia, with hazards of the Communist system and a secret handover of records.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah. Have you ever been a band leader per se? Like I know you have been on T.V.
Yeah, you are talking about in the sense of going around the country.

The closest I got to being a traditional on-the-road band leader was when I was directing the group which was then called “The New York Jazz Repertory Company” and we went to Russia, the Soviet Union that is, it wasn’t just Russia. And this was in 1975 and it was a remarkable experience. We did our Louis Armstrong show, which we had done previously in Carnegie Hall. In Moscow, Novorossiysk, which is way the heck over North of India, Alma Ata, which is in the south now, and Kazakhstan, all these places which are coming into the news now unfortunately, and one or two other spots. And we toured in buses or on maybe once or twice on a Russian plane. And it was an amazing introduction to the hazards and hardships of being a leader of a big band, doing that in Russia.
If you can do it there, you’d probably be able to do it anywhere, right?

Well one of the problems was vodka, we’ll say no more. And another was the fact that, although we were treated beautifully and everybody loved the music, ironically in far greater numbers than that concert drew or could draw even now in the U.S., we did run into some hazards of the Communist system. One time a bus couldn’t leave at a certain point because a towel was missing. Somebody had stolen state property. You have to be very tricky, but you were in a situation where the government owns the towels. That literally happened. And then there were other cases where those people were under such a yoke at the time. There were jazz fans and we all wanted to be as friendly as we could to them, and I remember there was a guy who was the head of the jazz club in Yaroslavl, which is a city north of Moscow. We wanted to give him some records. It wasn’t legal for him to accept records from us. We met in the park and we slipped them to him. Without saying a word, we put them from underneath our coat to underneath his coat, and he walked away as fast as he could. It was a moment out of classic espionage and that’s exactly what happened. That kind of thing was a kind of normal style of living for them, and it just amazed us.
